newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Latin America -- mired in past at door of 21st Century.
newsitem.headline: Latin America -- mired in past at door of 21st Century.

text.p: At the height of Ecuador's political crisis last week an admirer of embattled President Abdala Bucaram complained that the impoverished South American country was suddenly awash in bad press.
"At least they're paying attention," the volatile populist shot back, according to local media reports.

What went largely unnoticed, however, was how Bucaram's unceremonious ouster just a few days later contradicted what investment bankers and Wall Street gurus have been saying about Latin America for years.

The spin artists say Latin America has undergone a great leap forward toward stability, open markets and democratic rule -- factors that make it one of the most economically viable areas of the world.

But in a way, just as the peso crisis and myriad scandals that erupted after Carlos Salinas left Mexico's presidency in 1994, Bucaram's mercurial fall underscored how little things have changed in a region torn by decades of coups, guerrilla wars and extreme poverty.
At best, in the words of one Western diplomat, instead of a leap it has taken "one step back for every two it moves forward with."

Bucaram, an old school politician to be sure, was voted out of office by Ecador's Congress on Feb. 6 on grounds of "mental incompetence." Lawmakers offered the descendant of Lebanese immigrants no chance to defend himself in an impeachment trial.

And they failed to take notice of the fact that Ecuador's constitution is extremely vague on an issue as basic as who should succeed a sitting president -- opening the door to the fact that three people, including Bucaram, could then stake legitimate claims to the presidency.

Bucaram relinquished his claim before dawn last Sunday, but only after Ecuador's armed forces -- who proved to be the final arbiter of power in Ecuador -- brokered a bizarre agreement with his two would-be successors allowing both of them to occupy the presidential palace, albeit briefly.

There has been no response from the military high command to Bucaram's charges that it "intervened politically" in the crisis that saw his government booted out after just six months in office. The move followed a massive two-day strike against harsh economic austerity measures Bucaram unveiled in late December and early January.

Arturo Porzecanski, a veteran Latin American hand and chief economist for the Americas at ING Barings in New York, said things are looking up in Ecuador since the days when Bucaram pulled a gun on a fellow lawmaker to settle dispute on the floor of Congress.

"There's no more shootout at the O.K. Corral," he said, stressing that the military had only intervened behind-the- scenes in Ecuador and that ways of handling institutional conflicts in Latin America had "improved a great deal" in a short period of time.

He conceded that while "Latin America is very legalistic in general" it has a long tradition of violating laws on paper, however, and that Bucaram may have a point in calling his ouster a military-baced "congressional coup."
"When there is a big confrontation between the letter of the law and realities -- political or economic -- the letter of the law tends to suffer," Porzecanski said.

Other political analysts like Juan Tokatlian of the National University in Bogota, Colombia, say there is little real difference between Ecuador -- or Latin America -- today and what it was more than 40 years ago. He likened Bucaram, who has vowed to run for re-election in 2002, to Jose Maria Velasco Ibarra, another populist who was elected Ecuadorean president three times, the last in 1968, and was twice deposed by the military.
"Stability has never been something that Latin American was known for," Tokatlian said, adding that instability was something that stretches irrevocably from Tijuana to Tierra del Fuego.

"The only thing that's changed is the geography of stability and instability in Latin America," he said. Drugs and guerrilla wars and corruption have conspired to make the Andean region the hot spot in the late 1980s and 1990s, whereas Central America and the Caribbean held the spotlight in the 1970s and early 1980s.

The military dictatorships of the so-called "Suthern Coner" countries -- Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay and Chile -- were the centrepiece of attention long before Nicaragua, El Salvador, Grenada and Guatemala, he said.
"There's no real stability in Latin American," Tokatlian added. "There's never been any in the last 40 years."

Many analysts say the gradual opening of Latin America's economies, and the winds of democratic change sweeping across the region since the last 1970s and early 80s, provide solid hope for stability and deep-rooted political change.
But Sandy Markwik of Controlled Risks Group Ltd said governmnent institutions are still weak thoughout Latin America, and volatility is likely to be with it for some time.
"There's reasonable stability now from the investors point of view," Markwik said. "The problems of inequalty and policy will take decades to address."
